extracted.intended_audience: amateur naturalists, schoolchildren and beginner shell-collectors interested in British land and freshwater molluscs
extracted.subtask_description: Practical field-guide guidance for finding, identifying, collecting, killing, cleaning, labelling, packing, and storing British land and freshwater shells (and preserving slugs), aimed at beginners and amateur collectors. Emphasises necessary habits, tools, habitats, seasonal/timing tips, and preservation techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good naturalist/collector
rubrics_metrics.description: The habits of observation, of comparison, and of method are those which all naturalists and collectors must have; one must have the seeing eye, learn to observe small but important differences, and cultivate order, method and neatness in arranging collections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate the seeing eye (notice things others don't); learn to discriminate between similar objects (use magnifier/dissection when necessary); keep an ordered, neat collection; persistence (fortitude) is valuable—stick with collecting to build a complete series rather than fleetingly collecting many things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential field tools and kit
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry a magnifying glass (always in your pocket), a note-book, and, where possible, a microscope at home; for searching use a net, inverted umbrella (beating hedges), perforated scoop on a long stick for dredging, tin boxes, calico bag, small glass tubes with corks, and a lantern for night searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use glass tubes for tinier shells; calico bags with foliage for land shells; tin boxes with moss for freshwater shells; bring small glass tubes (homœopathic medicine bottles) to keep tiny specimens separate and safe; have a fine but strong jet of cold water available at home to wash out slime or particles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search (habitat rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Snails require lime to make shells and are abundant on chalk or limestone; search hedges (turn stones/branches/old boots/newspaper), smooth beech trunks, mossy tree bases, walls, damp places, ditches, ponds and backwaters for freshwater species, sand-hills and road-edges for certain hedgerow species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Box Hill and Caterham (chalk) vs Oxshott (sand) example; during hibernation (Nov–Apr) search ditches rather than hedges; look under stones, dead wood, newspaper, hurdles leaning on hedges; open traps like old flat wood or cardboard on grass to attract species that shelter under them.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to search (timing and seasonality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some snails hide or hibernate in winter; rainy days (especially followed by a warm evening), early morning, and night searches with a lantern are often most productive; the hibernating season extends from November to April when dredging ditches is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many species come out after rain; some only appear at night or in wet conditions; use these temporal cues to plan expeditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner species selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginners should first be directed to the common, beautiful, and variable hedge species Helix (Cepæa) nemoralis and H. (Tachea) hortensis, since they are common, show much variation, and are instructive for learning colour and band variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with species that are abundant and variable to learn to recognise range of variation; novices learn more quickly from common, conspicuous taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting specimens (live vs dead; size and condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases 'live shells,' i.e. shells in which the animal is alive, are to be chosen; when these cannot be procured, 'dead shells' which have not lost their lustre or colour are acceptable; only adult shells should usually be taken, and weather-worn or bleached specimens should be neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that in some cases the tiniest land shells and young imperfect shells should still be collected; experience is required to discriminate age/sex/maturity where young of one species resemble adults of another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field collecting techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn over stones, bricks, branches, dead wood or other cover; sweep herbage; beat hedges over an inverted umbrella; set simple traps (flat pieces of old wood or cardboard); use dredging and sifting in water with a perforated scoop on a stick to find freshwater species; search trunks (smooth beech bark), moss at tree bases, and the tops of walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For some sun-loving species provide newspaper as shelter/food; handfuls of dead leaves can be shaken over a white sheet or taken home for sorting; dredging and sifting like 'gold-washers' will reveal bivalves and univalves from bottom mud and weeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimen transport containers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a calico bag with a little foliage for land shells, tin boxes with a little moss for freshwater shells, and small glass tubes with corks for tinier kinds (homœopathic bottles are suggested).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep tiny shells separate and safe in tubes; for transport arrange packets without pressure with heavy shells at the bottom and fill blank spaces with paper or other elastic material; avoid sawdust as it injures lustre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field labelling and note-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry a notebook and record the species or varieties, the place where shells were found, dates of earliest/latest activity, observed habits, food plants, effects of weather on shell thickness, and anything noteworthy about protective colouring or mimicry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the name and place on a small slip of card placed in the tube or tray with the specimen; in dredging note the depth of water. Detailed notes aid later identification and scientific value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of magnification and dissection for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: A magnifying glass is necessary in many cases to separate similar kinds, and a microscope opens many lines of inquiry (e.g., study of mollusc teeth, radula, and minute anatomical points) which can determine whether two molluscs are the same species when shell shape is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study love-darts, teeth counts of the radula, mantle and soft anatomy, and other micro-characters; dissections and microscopic study are sometimes required where outward appearance is ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical characters to check
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters useful for differentiation include presence/absence of operculum, position of breathing orifice (in front of/behind centre of mantle margin), shell umbilicus, shape and sculpture of shell, love-darts, tentacle/eye placement, radula tooth counts, and features of soft anatomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: H. nemoralis vs H. hortensis may be distinguished by internal flinty dart; Arion vs Limax differences include shield texture, breathing orifice position, presence/absence of dorsal keel, and shell rudiment presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Killing and initial preparation of land and freshwater shells
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash of quite boiling water kills instantaneously any molluscs whose shells we want to preserve, after which the body is extracted; then wash out any slime or particles with a fine but strong jet of cold water into the shell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold thumb nearly over the mouth of a water-tap to concentrate the jet; ensure all body is removed; boiling water should not be used with marine shells as it often destroys their lustre. Alternatively shells may be drowned in cold water and hung up to dry if preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Killing and preserving slugs
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserving slugs is difficult; best is to have a coloured drawing made when extended; otherwise drown in cold water, clean slime with a soft brush, and preserve in glass tubes with diluted formalin or alcohol; or skin and dry the skins on a card and varnish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slugs often vary in colour; if preserving whole, dilute formalin or alcohol recommended. For Testacella and other subterranean species look for them on damp nights or when digging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning and avoiding damage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to clean shells beyond removing mud or sand with a soft brush; take care not to injure the lip of univalves or the ligament of bivalves; if bivalves gape on dying, close and tie the valves together; if ligament becomes dry and stiff soften by putting in water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When removing internal matter, wash thoroughly and replace operculum on cotton filling the shell if necessary; be cautious of actions that will damage edges or ligaments which are diagnostic features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packing shells for transport
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrap solid shells in one or two folds of paper; fragile and minute shells should be put separately into a box or bottle with or without cotton; arrange heavy shells at the bottom without pressure and fill blanks at the top with paper or elastic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sawdust because it injures lustre; use appropriate cushioning; small tubes/bottles are good for tiny species; ensure opercula are secured or shells closed to prevent damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage and arrangement of collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a cabinet is obtained, tiny shells in glass tubes with corks, medium shells in matchbox trays arranged in large shallow glass-covered trays stacked one above the other make a good temporary cabinet; keep the collection free from damp and dust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label each tube or tray with name and place found; if mounting shells on card, gum tragacanth is best; do not fasten unless necessary; choose storage that prevents mould/damp and preserves lustre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference and literature guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain good identification and reference books early in a collector's career (recommended: The Collector’s Manual by L. E. Adams; Rimmers’ Land and Fresh Water Shells) which give minute descriptions, varieties, and plates of illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authoritative manuals to confirm identifications and learn diagnostic characters; borrow or consult local collectors to learn by sight and practice as well as reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection ethics and provenance cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that many British shells are local; continental specimens often have varieties named as separate species—exercise caution when receiving shells from the Continent, and record locality as names and status may differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label locality accurately; treat continental identifications with skepticism as taxonomic practices vary by region; do not assume presence in Britain without locality evidence (e.g., pomatia often local or escape from captivity).
